title: Two Funerals

jokes.text: Ben gives the group a signal to cheer for Leslie's announcement, which turns out to be the extremely dry 'Senior Executive Service Development Candidate Program at the Department of the Interior'
jokes.setup: Ben hypes the group: 'she's gonna say something that sounds very boring but is actually a really big deal' — implying the signal will be for something exciting
jokes.punchline: The announcement is a mouthful of bureaucratic jargon that perfectly embodies 'sounds very boring,' and the group cheers wildly anyway
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks setup — Leslie's obsession with government bureaucracy played for warmth and comedy simultaneously. Ben's pre-framing is the perfect meta-commentary. The joke is fully character-integrated: only Leslie would be genuinely thrilled about this title. Good structure with the signal payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Leslie's about to make an announcement, and it's going to be boring as hell.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I'm going to make it exciting. I've got a marching band, I've got confetti cannons, I've got a guy dressed as a bald eagle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Making your announcement awesome!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just announcing the new community garden initiative.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: See? Boring. But with this setup, people will think it's important.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It IS important.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, but nobody cares about community gardens. They care about spectacle. So I'm giving them spectacle.

jokes.text: Garry announces his retirement and is immediately told 'This is about people who are moving, Garry. Not everything is about you.'
jokes.setup: Multiple cast members make exciting life announcements (promotion, new house). Garry announces his retirement.
jokes.punchline: He is shot down as if his retirement is a selfish derailment, when it's actually also significant news — the irony being that everyone else's announcements are equally self-focused
jokes.explanation: Classic Garry joke — he's always minimized. The irony is sharp: everyone else's announcements ARE about them, but Garry alone gets scolded. Character-integrated and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, we're here to make moving announcements. Who's first?

dialogue.speaker: Garry
dialogue.line: I'd like to announce my retirement.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Garry, that's not a moving announcement. That's completely off-topic.

jokes.text: 'Also I'm retiring.' / 'That's three, Garry.'
jokes.setup: Ben counts three announcements as 'bad news comes in threes' — Leslie/Ben, April/Andy, Donna. Then tries to pivot to good news.
jokes.punchline: Garry tries again to announce his retirement and is again dismissed as merely being the third item on someone else's list
jokes.explanation: The callback lands harder than the original setup. The economy is excellent — four words demolish Garry's milestone a second time. The escalation of the indignity is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so we have three major problems: the budget shortfall, the flooding in the south quadrant, and Garry's retirement.

dialogue.speaker: Garry
dialogue.line: Wait, my retirement is a major problem?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, Garry. It's right up there with municipal infrastructure collapse.

jokes.text: The news anchor begins 'Good evening. I come to you tonight with some good news...' then pivots: 'Is not a sentence I will be saying to you right now, because beloved Pawnee Mayor Walter Gunderson has died.'
jokes.setup: Ben says 'we're probably due for some good news' — cut to news anchor starting a sentence that promises good news
jokes.punchline: The anchor uses a syntactic trick to deliver the exact opposite — structurally subverts the expectation with a grammar twist
jokes.explanation: A clever structural subversion — the anchor literally begins the sentence you expect then uses grammar to negate it. The editing juxtaposition (Ben predicts good news → immediate cut to this) adds a layer. Original construction, well-executed. The 'is not a sentence I will be saying' construction is genuinely witty writing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're due for some good news.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The mayor just died.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Garry, why would you say that?

jokes.text: 'Well, you jinxed us, Garry. Thanks a lot.'
jokes.setup: Garry is blamed for the mayor's death because he mentioned bad news comes in threes and tried to count his retirement as one of them
jokes.punchline: The logical absurdity of blaming Garry for a death is played straight, extending his role as perpetual scapegoat
jokes.explanation: Functional Garry joke. Blaming him for a death is an escalation of the running gag. Not particularly original but character-integrated and lands because the show has earned this dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: News Reporter
dialogue.line: Mayor's body will lie in state in council chambers.

jokes.text: Mayor Gunderson's pre-recorded farewell video: 'I wasn't paying attention most of the time. Fortunately, the citizens of Pawnee didn't pay attention either.'
jokes.setup: A solemn posthumous video message from the mayor about his legacy
jokes.punchline: He admits to complete dereliction of duty, then praises the citizens for also not noticing — mutual negligence as civic harmony
jokes.explanation: The posthumous confession structure is inherently funny, but the specific observation — that citizens not paying attention is a feature, not a bug, of his tenure — is an incisive satirical point about local government. Good economy and a genuine comic idea.

dialogue.speaker: Mayor Gunderson
dialogue.line: Citizens of Pawnee, if you're watching this, I am dead. I want you to know that every good thing that happened in this town was because of me. The new library? Me. The park expansion? Me. The low crime rate? All me. However, if anything bad has happened, that is entirely your fault. The pothole on Elm Street? You didn't report it properly. The budget deficit? You spend too much. The decline in property values? You didn't maintain your homes. I was a great mayor, and I regret nothing.

jokes.text: 'Good-bye forever.'
jokes.setup: A formal posthumous video message ending
jokes.punchline: 'Good-bye forever' — technically accurate (he's dead) but bluntly comedic in its finality
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective capper to the Gunderson video. The literalness of 'forever' (since he's dead) combined with the casual delivery makes it land. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We need something to begin - an underground dance competition.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have no idea how to do it, but I'm assuming you guys do.

jokes.text: Leslie declares they need something to begin and proposes 'an underground dance competition,' then immediately admits 'I'm realizing I know nothing about the logistics of how to start an underground dance competition'
jokes.setup: Leslie, in problem-solving mode, announces a bold plan
jokes.punchline: She immediately walks it back with a total lack of follow-through knowledge — rare moment of Leslie self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A small but authentic Leslie character moment. The joke is in the contrast between her confident declaration and immediate admission of ignorance. Works because Leslie's competence is usually unimpeachable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I have mayoral experience from when I was mayor of Ice Town.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You drove the entire town into bankruptcy by investing all the municipal funds into an ice skating rink in a desert. It was called Ice Town. You made Ice Town.

jokes.text: 'Oh, yeah, you completely disgraced yourself and destroyed an entire town.' / 'Yeah, I said we all remember.'
jokes.setup: Ben mentions he was mayor once before and it didn't go well — 'we all remember how that went'
jokes.punchline: April states the disaster in its full brutal specificity; Ben's deadpan 'yeah, I said we all remember' refuses to engage further
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: April's brutal specificity ('destroyed an entire town') and Ben's flat refusal to relitigate it. Both are in character. The callback to Ice Town rewards longtime viewers. Ben's deadpan is perfectly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: I'm going to notarize the new mayor's documents. This is the most important thing I've ever done.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great, Gary!

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: I know. You could say I'm about to make things... Legally Blond-knope.

jokes.text: Garry being excited that notarizing a new mayor is 'the ultimate notary adventure' — 'Oh, it's big.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells Garry he can help find a new mayor. Garry is given the consolation task of notarizing.
jokes.punchline: Garry receives this with genuine awe — 'the ultimate notary adventure' — treating a mundane bureaucratic task as a life peak
jokes.explanation: A well-observed Garry beat — his genuine enthusiasm for the most mundane possible task is endearing and funny. 'Oh, it's big' as a reaction to notarizing is perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: April, I got you these men's loafers. They're very comfortable and very professional.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm a woman.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know that. These are unisex loafers.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, they're not.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I think I bought these for myself.

jokes.text: Tom greets Leslie with 'Les-legally Blonde!' and presents her with Men's Ferragamo loafers — 'What am I supposed to do with these?' / 'Yeah, you're right. I should probably keep them. They're a size 6 1/2. Too small for you anyway.'
jokes.setup: Tom returns from New York with a gift for Leslie, building anticipation
jokes.punchline: The gift is men's luxury shoes in his own size — he immediately reclaims them while insulting her feet
jokes.explanation: Tom gifting himself while framing it as generosity is perfect Tom character comedy. The 'too small for you anyway' adds insult to injury. 'Les-legally Blonde' is a fun wordplay greeting. Fully character-integrated — this could only be Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I was looking at rings in jewelry stores the other day. You know who makes great jewelry? Shia LaBeouf. Yeah, Shia LaBeouf designs jewelry now. Just DO IT. Just buy the ring.

jokes.text: 'Shia LaBeouf is one hell of a jewelry designer, by the way. Man's really found his calling.'
jokes.setup: Tom is describing his romantic trip to New York with Lucy, including looking at rings
jokes.punchline: A completely unexpected name-drop of Shia LaBeouf as a jewelry designer — presented as sincere praise for his 'calling'
jokes.explanation: The absurdist celebrity name-drop works because it's so specific and delivered with total sincerity. 'Man's really found his calling' as a genuine compliment to Shia LaBeouf the jeweler is a funny idea. Somewhat dependent on the audience's familiarity with LaBeouf's erratic public persona.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You could propose to her at the memorial!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, no, that's completely inappropriate.

jokes.text: 'What better place to ask a woman to marry you than an old man's public memorial?'
jokes.setup: Leslie, caught up in romantic momentum, encourages Tom to propose to Lucy right now, at the mayor's memorial
jokes.punchline: She articulates the absurdity of her own suggestion with cheerful obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Leslie's romantic enthusiasm overriding basic situational awareness is a classic character beat. The line is self-aware but still feels in character — she's not joking, she genuinely thinks this might work. The phrase 'old man's public memorial' is a well-chosen specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The mayor has been in office for like, what, thirty years? That's a long postulence of time.

jokes.text: Andy uses the word 'postulence' — 'Really makes you consider the postulence of time.'
jokes.setup: Andy reflects solemnly on Mayor Gunderson's 39-year tenure
jokes.punchline: 'Postulence' — a nonsense word delivered with complete sincerity, clearly a mangled attempt at 'obsolescence' or 'transience'
jokes.explanation: Andy's confident use of a made-up word is pure character comedy. The joke is entirely in the delivery — he has no idea. 'Sure.' as the response (presumably from April or someone) is the perfect deadpan acknowledgment. Fully Andy-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Life is just a series of moments until you die. It's not that bad, actually. You're born, you take some time to figure out what you're doing, then you die. In between, you can do whatever you want, which is nice. But mostly you're just waiting to die.

jokes.text: April: 'Death is natural, Andrew. We're born, we survive as long as we're useful, and then we're killed, either by our body's natural decay or by those younger and stronger.'
jokes.setup: A moment of reflection at the mayor's lying in state — expecting platitudes
jokes.punchline: April delivers a Darwinian/nihilistic worldview with complete calm, treating murder by younger competitors as a natural death option
jokes.explanation: Peak April. The pivot from 'natural decay' to 'killed by those younger and stronger' as equivalent options is the comedic turn. Fully character-integrated — this worldview is 100% April Ludgate. The deadpan delivery implied by the transcript makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, death is just a natural part of life. But you know what? If we save up enough money, we could get cryogenically frozen, and then in like 200 years, they'll have robot bodies, and we can just keep on balling forever!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, right?

jokes.text: Andy: 'Before I die, I'm freezing my head like Ted Williams. Wait a thousand years, thaw it out, slap it on a robot, keep on balling.'
jokes.setup: April delivers her grim philosophy about death; Andy responds
jokes.punchline: Andy's immortality plan is a cascade of absurdity: cryonics → robot body → 'keep on balling' — the last phrase being both vague and perfectly Andy
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent Andy comedy. The logic has internal consistency (Ted Williams reference is real), but 'slap it on a robot, keep on balling' is the perfect absurdist escalation. 'Keep on balling' as Andy's ultimate life goal is character-perfect. Quotable and specific. One of the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so Salvatore's dead? April said he was the strongest man alive!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He was. Until he wasn't.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is... if I want to survive, I should become a barber?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not what I said.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, no, I get it. Barbers live forever. That's why my grandpa kept going to the same barber for 50 years.

jokes.text: Ron learns mid-conversation that his barber Salvatore has also died — 'What? What happened? Explain yourself!'
jokes.setup: Ron stoically attends the mayor's memorial. Carl mentions it's terrible, 'first Salvatore and now Mayor Gunderson.'
jokes.punchline: Ron is completely blindsided — he had no idea his barber died, and his reaction ('Explain yourself!') suggests this loss hits harder than the mayor's
jokes.explanation: Excellent character reveal. Ron's priorities are perfectly calibrated — he's at a mayoral memorial but the barber death hits him harder. 'Explain yourself!' as a response to news of a death is both funny and revealing. Sets up the entire Salvatore subplot. Strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: I met Mayor Gunderson forty-three years ago at a regional water treatment conference in Indianapolis. We had an immediate connection over our shared passion for municipal infrastructure and... well, other things.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: For four decades, I was his closest confidant. His most trusted advisor. The woman he called at three in the morning when he needed to talk about his dreams, his fears, and his marriage—which, as many of you know, was quite loveless.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: I stood by him through every campaign, every scandal, every difficult decision. I was there when his wife wasn't. Literally, I was in the room. Many rooms, actually. Hotel rooms, mostly.

jokes.text: Andy asks: 'Was he killed by a younger, stronger barber?'
jokes.setup: Ron is devastated to learn his barber died
jokes.punchline: Andy callbacks April's earlier Darwinian death philosophy and applies it literally to the barber's death
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect callback. Andy takes April's dark philosophy and applies it with earnest literalness to a barber's death. The specificity ('younger, stronger barber') makes it funnier than a generic callback. Shows Andy actually absorbed what April said without fully understanding it. Economy is superb — nine words deliver the whole joke. Justifiably one of the episode's best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: Graphic sexual details followed by calling the audience prudes

jokes.text: Ethel Beavers begins her eulogy: 'I'll be brief. Walter Gunderson and his wife had an open marriage.'
jokes.setup: Solemn public memorial, Ethel introduced as the mayor's 'longtime friend and coworker.' The preamble is 'This is gonna be so sad.'
jokes.punchline: 'I'll be brief. Walter Gunderson and his wife had an open marriage.' — the complete tonal whiplash from expected eulogy to revealing a 46-year affair
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant. 'I'll be brief' promises mercy; 'Walter Gunderson and his wife had an open marriage' is the exact opposite of brevity in terms of what it opens up. The setup ('longtime friend and coworker') and the foreshadowing ('this is gonna be so sad') make the misdirection complete. Economy of language is exceptional — the punchline is one sentence that blows up the scene. Standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: I loved him for more than sex.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: I also loved him for his big, strong...

jokes.text: Ethel waves to Evelyn in the crowd while delivering the eulogy about the open marriage
jokes.setup: Ethel is describing the open marriage arrangement that 'kept everyone happy'
jokes.punchline: She casually waves to Evelyn — presumably the wife — mid-revelation, implying they all know each other and are fine with this
jokes.explanation: A visual beat that escalates the absurdity — the casual 'Hi, Evelyn' wave implies a weirdly functional arrangement that makes the whole thing even funnier. Inferred from 'Hi, Evelyn' in the transcript.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: I love the mayor. He's an animal.

jokes.text: Ethel says 'because for 46 wonderful years, he spent night after night exploring every nook and cranny of my body' — then breaks the fourth wall slightly: 'Grow up, you prudes. We're all adults.'
jokes.setup: Ethel has been escalating the revelation of her 46-year affair with the dead mayor, at his public memorial
jokes.punchline: 'Every nook and cranny' as a euphemism followed by 'grow up, you prudes' — the elderly woman scolding the audience for being shocked at a funeral
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'nook and cranny' is a perfectly calibrated euphemism — explicit enough to be uncomfortable, vague enough for broadcast. 'Grow up, you prudes' flips the dynamic so Ethel becomes the judging party. The moral authority she claims while saying this is the comic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you want for your proposal?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I want it to be like an action movie. You know, where the hero defeats the villain and saves the day? Except the hero is me. Tom Haverford. And the villain is... loneliness. I defeat loneliness by proposing to the woman I love. And then there's an explosion. A huge explosion. In slow motion. And I'm walking away from it, not looking back, because I'm cool. And my name appears on the screen in big letters: TOM HAVERFORD. Tom Haverford in... Love. Coming this fall.

jokes.text: 'And not just because he was a dynamite lay. Good night, you animal.'
jokes.setup: Ethel says her one regret is not telling him how she really felt — then says 'I loved that man.'
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies the love with 'not just because he was a dynamite lay' — then closes with 'Good night, you animal' as her tender farewell
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic peak. 'Dynamite lay' is the perfectly chosen period slang — specific, character-appropriate for an older woman, and just crass enough. 'Good night, you animal' as a tender eulogy closer is genuinely brilliant writing — it's simultaneously affectionate and explicit, and the phrase 'you animal' at a public memorial is the perfect button. Highly quotable. This line alone justifies Ethel's character existence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need that banner by tomorrow morning or I will personally come to your house and make one myself out of your furniture.

dialogue.speaker: Banner Maker
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'll have it ready.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you. Also, I'm going to need seventeen more banners for next week.

dialogue.speaker: Banner Maker
dialogue.line: Ms. Knope, I'm concerned about your banner spending. Have you considered talking to someone?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A therapist? I don't have time for that. I have banners to order.

jokes.text: Tom describes his ideal proposal as 'a multiplatform media experience, an action movie with explosive graphics, fast cars, and a hero with one mission — to propose to his lady. A hero named... Tom Haverford.'
jokes.setup: Leslie urges Tom to propose, asking what he wants to do
jokes.punchline: Tom's ideal proposal is a Hollywood action movie starring himself — his vanity extended to the most intimate moment
jokes.explanation: Tom wanting to be the hero of his own cinematic proposal is perfectly in character. The dramatic pause before 'Tom Haverford' as the hero's name is a strong structural beat. His self-mythologizing has never been more absurdly articulated.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: How's Leslie doing?

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Wait, what office were you guys running for again?

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: You know what, it doesn't matter. Politics is so boring.

jokes.text: Tom on the phone: 'If you can't train 200 white doves in the next four hours to spell out "Lucy, will you marry me?" then you have no business calling yourself a pet store.'
jokes.setup: Tom is executing his elaborate proposal plan
jokes.punchline: Demanding that a pet store train 200 doves to spell out words in four hours, framed as a basic professional competency
jokes.explanation: The logic is perfectly Tom — the outrage isn't that doves can't spell, but that the pet store isn't up to the task. 'No business calling yourself a pet store' as a professional critique of an impossible request is a well-constructed absurdist line.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: I can't be mayor. I'm going to space next week. I already booked my ticket on Virgin Galactic.

jokes.text: Leslie explains to the banner store owner that her credit card company called — 'not to question the charges but to sincerely ask me if I was mentally stable'
jokes.setup: Leslie is leveraging her 15 years of banner orders and $100,000 spent to get a last-minute favor
jokes.punchline: Her spending is so extreme that her credit card company called not for fraud concerns but for mental health concerns
jokes.explanation: This is sharp, economical character comedy. The twist — the call is about mental stability, not fraud — recontextualizes the banner obsession as something even more extreme than financial recklessness. Fully character-specific to Leslie. The pivot from 'not to question the charges' to the real reason is a clean misdirection. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Space travel is fascinating. I've always wanted to go to space.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm Buzz Aldrin.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Oh, like from Toy Story?

jokes.text: 'See that Rolex Submariner on your wrist, bro? That's 'cause of Leslie. You'll have the banner done.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is negotiating with the banner store owner who says the order is impossible
jokes.punchline: She points to his luxury watch as direct evidence of their relationship's value — a mob-adjacent negotiation tactic from Leslie Knope
jokes.explanation: Leslie leveraging her banner spending as power is funny — the Rolex as proof of their transactional relationship casts Leslie as an unlikely power player. 'Bro' from Leslie is also a small comedy tick.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I go to the same barber every week. We don't talk much. He cuts my hair, I pay him, I leave. The perfect conversation is about nothing at all.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport can't remember what office Leslie ran for: 'How's Leslie? Is she still, um... uh... Oh. What was that thing we ran for again?' / 'City councilor.' / 'I don't know. All right, if you say so.'
jokes.setup: Ben and April meet with potential mayor candidates. Bobby Newport, Leslie's old rival, appears.
jokes.punchline: He can't remember what office they both ran for — and shrugs off the answer when told
jokes.explanation: Perfect Bobby Newport character consistency. His cluelessness about the very election he ran in is both funny and a precise character reminder for returning viewers. 'I don't know. All right, if you say so.' is the ideal capstone — he doesn't even accept the answer with certainty.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Will collect change from the barber's widow

jokes.text: Bobby Newport: 'I can't do it, though... I'm getting ready to go on a big trip, to space.' / 'That'll be really fun too.' / 'Everything in life is always just so fun, right?' / 'It really is.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks Bobby to be interim mayor for two months — a low-stakes civic duty
jokes.punchline: Bobby can't do it because he's going to space — said with zero irony, and Ben's earnest validation ('That'll be really fun too') is the comedy
jokes.explanation: Bobby's offhand 'I'm going to space' and Ben's polite 'that'll be really fun too' creates a perfect comedic rhythm of two people with completely different reference frames agreeing cordially. 'Everything in life is always just so fun' as Bobby's worldview is a great character note.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I consider this wildly unkempt. Like a rock star.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport: 'Everything in life is always just so fun, right?' — then inviting Ben to space, pitching the Russian rocket guys as 'cool with it'
jokes.setup: Bobby is musing about how fun everything is
jokes.punchline: He casually invites Ben to join him in space and assures him the Russian rocket engineers would be 'cool with it' — as if it's an Airbnb situation
jokes.explanation: The 'Russian guys would be cool with it' framing is funny — treating a billion-dollar space program as if it's a casual carpool. Bobby's sunny obliviousness continues to pay off.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I created an elaborate backstory for a one-line role.

jokes.text: Buzz Aldrin appears and says 'I was the second person to walk on the moon. Buzz Aldrin. Nice to meet you.' / 'Nice try. That's the guy from Toy Story.'
jokes.setup: Buzz Aldrin introduces himself as the second person to walk on the moon
jokes.punchline: Bobby Newport dismisses him as the cartoon character Buzz Lightyear, having no idea who Buzz Aldrin is
jokes.explanation: Brilliant deployment of a celebrity cameo. Buzz Aldrin's presence is already fun, but Bobby dismissing him as 'the guy from Toy Story' is a perfect encapsulation of Bobby's privileged ignorance. The specificity of 'Nice try' — as if Aldrin is an impostor — makes it even better. Highly quotable. The joke works on multiple levels: celebrity cameo, character comedy, and cultural commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Bonjour, I am a French woman who does karate.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You said the main character was French!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're replacing you with a stunt double.

jokes.text: Ron's tribute to Salvatore: the entire relationship described as 'Same exact thing every time. I paid him $8. I sat in the same chair... Then he'd always ask me about the same thing... nothing. It was perfect.'
jokes.setup: People ask if Ron was close with his barber Salvatore
jokes.punchline: Ron describes four decades of a relationship defined by absolute silence and routine — 'he'd always ask me about... nothing. It was perfect.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The buildup to 'he'd always ask me about...' with a pause before 'nothing' is a masterclass in comedic timing on the page. 'It was perfect' as the sincere conclusion captures Ron's character completely — a 40-year relationship of mutual silence as the ideal human connection. Character integration is as high as it gets. Fully earned, no cheap shortcuts.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to marry me.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional: 'The three most important people in a man's life are his barber, his butcher, and his lover. I have lost one of those.'
jokes.setup: Ron grieves the loss of his barber in a talking-head confessional
jokes.punchline: He lists three life pillars — then 'I have lost one of those' is deliberately ambiguous: is it the barber, butcher, or lover? (Context tells us it's the barber, which is the funny answer.)
jokes.explanation: Philosophically concise and perfectly Ron. Elevating a barber to the same status as a lover is the comic engine, and the spare 'I have lost one of those' — without specifying which — is excellent economy. The ambiguity is intentional and funny. Highly quotable and character-defining.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That action sequence was incredible! The way he jumped through that window, did a backflip, and landed perfectly on his feet!

dialogue.speaker: Jewelry Store Owner
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was MY storefront window. And those are MY display cases he landed on. That's $40,000 worth of merchandise!

jokes.text: Ron leaves $10 at the barber's coffin: 'As you know, I don't believe in tipping, so I will collect my change from your wife.'
jokes.setup: Ron pays his respects at Salvatore's coffin, leaving money
jokes.punchline: He clarifies he'll collect the $2 change from the widow — his no-tipping principle observed even at a funeral
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's very best jokes. The logic is airtight Ron Swanson: he pays the barber's established $8 rate, leaves $10 out of respect, but his anti-tipping principle means he must collect change — from the grieving widow, at a funeral. The 'As you know' addressing the corpse is also brilliant. Every element is character-specific, dark without being mean-spirited, and delivered with perfect economy. Comparable to top-tier Ron moments in the series.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, you're 27?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That means he was born in... oh my god.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're older than Bobby.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We've been taking life advice from someone younger than us.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'Look how raggedy my hair is. What am I supposed to be, some kind of rock star?'
jokes.setup: Ron has a scheduled haircut appointment that can't be kept because Salvatore is dead
jokes.punchline: Ron is distressed about his hair being slightly unkempt, describing it as 'raggedy' and implying that's only acceptable for rock stars
jokes.explanation: Ron's vanity about his conservative, unchanged hair is a good character detail. The rock star comparison as the only acceptable alternative to his precise look is funny. Efficient and character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not paying me? I performed!

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: I need five thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Actually, make it ten thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: No, fifty thousand. And a car. A Range Rover.

jokes.text: Leslie shows up as a character in Tom's proposal movie with an elaborate French backstory — 'I came up with a backstory for my character. She's married to a French billionaire, and she has a twin sister, identical, and they keep—' / 'Leslie, you have one line.'
jokes.setup: Tom has given Leslie a simple cameo role in his proposal video
jokes.punchline: Leslie has fully committed to an elaborate character with French accent, billionaire husband, and an identical twin — for a one-line role
jokes.explanation: Leslie's over-commitment to a bit is a reliable comedic vein. The escalation of the backstory (French, billionaire, identical twin, 'and they keep—') before being cut off is a well-timed comedic truncation. Character-specific: Leslie always does too much.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Inappropriate sexual comment with sound effect

jokes.text: The action movie proposal scene: Leslie breaks character to explain her French billionaire backstory with a twin sister
jokes.setup: Tom is filming an action movie proposal. Leslie plays a jewelry store clerk with one line.
jokes.punchline: 'Why are you doing an accent?' 'I came up with a backstory for my character. She's married to a French billionaire, and she has a twin sister, identical, and they keep—' 'Leslie, you have one line.'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's over-commitment to a minor role — complete with French accent and elaborate backstory cut off mid-sentence — is wonderful character work. She is constitutionally incapable of being a supporting player in anything. The escalation of 'twin sister, identical, and they keep—' being interrupted is a great truncated escalation gag.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Being mayor means you have to be nice to people all the time. You're going to get a stress rash, your eye's going to twitch, and you'll develop a drinking problem. But that's the job.

jokes.text: The film shoots a scene with 'stunt double' chaos, with Tom yelling 'Go, my puppets! Go, my puppets! / Fight, fight, my puppets!' while confused crew members execute his commands
jokes.setup: Tom is directing an action sequence for his proposal video with apparent stunt doubles
jokes.punchline: 'Go, my puppets!' repeated as a directorial command — Tom treating people as marionettes while pretending to be a serious action director
jokes.explanation: Primarily a visual comedy sequence. The 'Go, my puppets!' line works as a character beat — Tom's grandiosity — but the humor is largely dependent on what the audience sees (inferred from context). Functional, fun, but not the sharpest writing in the episode.

jokes.text: Tom's action movie climax — he narrates to Lucy over the video: 'Lucy, your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to marry me.'
jokes.setup: The elaborate action movie proposal has been building
jokes.punchline: The Mission: Impossible-style line applied to a marriage proposal — grandiose genre applied to a personal moment
jokes.explanation: The Mission: Impossible parody applied to a marriage proposal is a recognizable but well-executed joke. Not the most original concept, but executed with Tom-appropriate commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, where do I know you from?

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: We're in the same frisbee league.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh right! You're on that team with the awful name.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: That's rich coming from someone on the Disc-Ciples.

jokes.text: After the proposal video, the jewelry store owner Ted says 'No, it wasn't [amazing]. You just destroyed my case.' / Tom: 'Hey, it's the movie business, Ted. You knew the risks.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just filmed an action sequence in a jewelry store, apparently breaking merchandise
jokes.punchline: Tom treats the destruction of Ted's inventory as an accepted occupational hazard of being adjacent to Hollywood
jokes.explanation: 'You knew the risks' as a response to destroying someone's livelihood for a personal proposal video is perfectly Tom — his self-absorption is so complete he's reframed a jewelry store owner as a Hollywood player who accepted risk.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: We should turn to Eastern wisdom.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I have Eastern wisdom. It's called Scottish whisky.

jokes.text: Ben meets a very young mayoral candidate who says 'You should be President of the universe' / 'I really would make an incredible mayor. But, sadly, I cannot, because I'm only 27 years old.' / 'Really? So you were born in the 1990s?' / 'Ooh! Mmhmm.'
jokes.setup: A seemingly promising candidate is enthusiastic about being mayor
jokes.punchline: He's too young by law, and Ben's response ('So you were born in the 1990s?') — delivered as a dawning horror — gets a gleeful 'Mmhmm' from the candidate who treats his youth as charming
jokes.explanation: A solid observational joke about generational divide. Ben's existential horror at someone born in the 1990s is relatable. Not particularly original but the candidate's delighted 'Mmhmm' as a response is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Who cuts my hair? Nobody. I have a very close personal relationship with my hair. We communicate on a spiritual level. When it's time for it to go, it just... leaves. It's beautiful, really.

jokes.text: Another candidate declines because of 'my practice, my other businesses, my two terrible children'
jokes.setup: Candidate listing reasons she can't be mayor
jokes.punchline: 'My two terrible children' listed flatly alongside professional obligations — casual parental honesty
jokes.explanation: A small but clean joke. The candor of 'terrible' as a parental descriptor lands in the deadpan — it's the kind of honest admission that gets a genuine laugh. Brief and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You hate me, Ron? Well, I don't hate you. I love you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm gonna kill you.

jokes.text: The Douche (a shock-jock DJ) enters and immediately says 'I'm gonna turn the mayoral office into my oral office.' / 'What?' / 'My oral office! Boom! Thought of it a second ago, had to pop back in. Had to?'
jokes.setup: The Douche is being considered for interim mayor and seems more qualified than expected
jokes.punchline: He has already figured out his inaugural pun — 'oral office' for 'Oval Office' — and is so proud he returns just to deliver it
jokes.explanation: The joke isn't the pun itself but the character behavior: he leaves, thinks of it, comes back. 'Had to pop back in. Had to?' as a self-interrogating acknowledgment that he didn't have to but the pun compelled him is very funny character writing. The Douche is perfectly deployed.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, did you just call me cool?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I did.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh. Um. Thanks. That's... cool.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And just like that, you're awkward again.

jokes.text: The Douche's daughter performs a John Mayer impression: 'Daddy, someone set a fire in your car / Because you took too long and I got bored'
jokes.setup: The Douche mentions his daughter is with him; she appears and announces she will 'do John Mayer'
jokes.punchline: Her John Mayer impression is a child singing about arson in an adult's car, framed as singer-songwriter blues
jokes.explanation: A child singing about setting her father's car on fire in the style of John Mayer is delightfully specific. The genre choice (mellow singer-songwriter confessional) for arson is the comedy. Inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You're cool, April.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Thanks. I mean, dope. Radical. That's tight, homie.

jokes.text: The Douche makes his case: 'I went to Northwestern, I've worked on two political campaigns, and I spend all of my time communicating with the public.' Then immediately adds: 'And some gross things with those juicy city hall interns. Ga-ga-goink!'
jokes.setup: The Douche is making a surprisingly compelling case for why he'd be a good mayor
jokes.punchline: The self-sabotage is immediate — 'and some gross things with those juicy city hall interns' plus the sound effect 'Ga-ga-goink' — he can't help himself
jokes.explanation: The structure is the joke: competent political resume followed instantly by disqualifying behavior he can't suppress. The sound effect 'Ga-ga-goink' as a self-authored punctuation mark is character-specific absurdism. The setup/subversion structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: You gotta propose to a lot of women to find the right one. It's like a numbers game, bro. I've proposed to like seventeen women, and I'm still looking for that special lady who says yes.

jokes.text: April tells Ben he should be mayor, then says: 'Ugh. Being nice made me feel terrible.'
jokes.setup: April gives Ben a genuine, heartfelt argument for why he should be mayor
jokes.punchline: Her immediate, physical revulsion at having been nice is the payoff — sincerity as something she has to recover from
jokes.explanation: Seven words of perfect April. The economy is exceptional — she articulates her discomfort with kindness more precisely than most characters could in a paragraph. The line captures April's entire character arc in a single complaint. Highly quotable and fully character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm about to become mayor and finally put the Ice Town thing behind me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But you know what? Ice Town was actually... it was a formative experience. It taught me resilience, humility, how to fail publicly and come back from it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ice Town made me who I am today. Without Ice Town, I wouldn't be here.

jokes.text: Ron confesses he's never been a fan of change. An unnamed stranger responds: 'In my experience, the only constant is change.' / Ron: 'Oh, shit.'
jokes.setup: Ron is having a moment of genuine vulnerability about change and loss
jokes.punchline: A stranger delivers the most banal philosophical cliché — and Ron's reaction ('Oh, shit') suggests it lands on him as profound wisdom he's never considered
jokes.explanation: The joke is Ron being hit hard by a greeting-card platitude. His 'Oh, shit' — implying it's a revelation — is funny because it recontextualizes the most tired saying in the world as genuinely affecting him. Works because we understand Ron as someone who avoids this kind of wisdom, so encountering it unexpectedly lands.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Jerry, I want to offer you the position of mayor.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No. No, absolutely not. I can't do that.

jokes.text: Ron asks the stranger if they've met; stranger says 'our souls have collided in one lifetime or another.' Ron: 'No, that's not it. Are you in my Frisbee golf league?'
jokes.setup: A mystical stranger offers a spiritual explanation for their connection
jokes.punchline: Ron rejects the spiritual explanation and offers the most mundane alternative: Frisbee golf
jokes.explanation: Ron deflating mysticism with Frisbee golf is a character-perfect move. The specificity of the Frisbee golf league is better than any generic alternative. He's not being dismissive; he's being practically Ron — he actually wants to place the guy.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: So you're engaged, huh? That's cool. You know what else is cool? Me. We should hang out sometime. Like, alone. In a dark room.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: I'm not saying I'm a parking ticket, but you've got FINE written all over you.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Are you a magician? Because whenever I look at you, everyone else disappears. Mostly because they're running away from us.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Do you believe in love at first sight, or should I walk by again? Actually, don't answer that. I'm just gonna stand here.

jokes.text: The mysterious stranger offers Ron 'Eastern wisdom' from 'the Isle of Islay in Scotland' — handing him a Scotch whisky.
jokes.setup: 'I've found it's best to turn to Eastern wisdom' — implying philosophy or meditation
jokes.punchline: He produces a bottle of Islay Scotch — 'this is as Eastern as my wisdom gets'
jokes.explanation: 'This is as Eastern as my wisdom gets' is a very clean misdirection payoff. The setup primes you for philosophy; the punchline reframes geography humorously. Also perfect for Ron, who would genuinely accept this as wisdom. The line is quotable on its own.

jokes.text: Ron asks who cuts the stranger's hair; stranger replies: 'Nobody. Whenever my hair feels it has completed its journey, it simply sheds itself off.' / 'I hate you so much.' / 'And I love you, my brother.'
jokes.setup: Ron needs a new barber and asks the mystical stranger who cuts his hair
jokes.punchline: The stranger delivers a transcendental explanation for hair loss disguised as intentional; Ron's hatred is the sincere punchline
jokes.explanation: 'It simply sheds itself off' as a mystical reframing of baldness is inventive. Ron's 'I hate you so much' — sincere, not playing — paired with the stranger's instant 'And I love you, my brother' creates a perfect two-person rhythm. The dynamic is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: So what do you do for fun, Typhoon?

dialogue.speaker: Typhoon
dialogue.line: I'm working on a sculptural series about the existential dread of modern bureaucracy. I'm using only reclaimed wood and the bones of animals I've hunted myself.

jokes.text: April says 'I'm a cool dudette' in response to Leslie calling her cool — and immediately Leslie says 'You've lost it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie shares a heartfelt moment with April, telling her she's 'pretty cool'
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a cool dudette' — April's deeply uncool response to being called cool, followed by instant judgment from Leslie
jokes.explanation: A light character moment. April trying to accept a compliment and fumbling it ('dudette') is consistent. The immediate reversal ('you've lost it') is quick and clean. Modest but functional.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Berlin is just a bunch of people on bikes complaining about things.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So basically it's Portland with a German accent and more history of being divided.

jokes.text: Tom's elaborate plan falls apart when he realizes 'We're calling this off. It's all wrong.' Lucy asks if it's because he said 'it's pizza time.' / 'No, but that definitely didn't help.'
jokes.setup: April and Tom's elaborate proposal plan begins collapsing
jokes.punchline: April's guess — that saying 'it's pizza time' was the problem — is both absurd and partially confirmed
jokes.explanation: 'No, but that definitely didn't help' is the perfectly calibrated response — it neither confirms nor denies, but acknowledges the insanity of saying 'it's pizza time' at a romantic moment. Tom's semi-validation is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need another banner made, and I need it NOW. This is urgent!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's a banner.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A banner that could change everything, Ron. I need to call in my banner guy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You have a banner guy?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Of course I do. Just like I have a caterer guy, an event guy, and a guy who knows a guy who can get us permits. Banner emergencies are no joke.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio adds flavored condoms to Tom's proposal kit — 'I didn't ask for flavored condoms.' 'No, no, no, that's just me looking out for you. See, girls get mad horny when you propose. That's why I do it all the time.'
jokes.setup: Tom has asked Jean-Ralphio and others to gather specific items for the proposal
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio added flavored condoms. His justification — that girls get horny at proposals, which is why he proposes 'all the time' — reveals his entire worldview in two sentences.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio at his most Jean-Ralphio. The reveal of WHY he added them is funnier than the condoms themselves — using proposals as a seduction strategy is a great character-consistent dark joke about his romantic ethics. 'That's why I do it all the time' is the punchy button.

dialogue.speaker: Garry
dialogue.line: I can't believe this is happening. Me, Garry Gergich, mayor of Pawnee. After all these years of being ignored and made fun of, I finally get my moment.

dialogue.speaker: Garry
dialogue.line: This is the best day of my life. Better than when I won employee of the month at the Parks Department. Better than my wedding day. Better than when my kids were born.

dialogue.speaker: Garry
dialogue.line: I'm actually the mayor. The mayor! Me!

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio: 'I didn't ask for flavored condoms.' / 'No, no, no, that's just me looking out for you. See, girls get mad horny when you propose. That's why I do it all the time.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Jean-Ralphio are gathering supplies for the new proposal
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio has added flavored condoms to the proposal supplies and defends it as insider knowledge — 'that's why I do it all the time' (he proposes constantly for this reason)
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio is one of the show's great recurring characters and this is a quintessential Jean-Ralphio beat. 'That's why I do it all the time' — implying he serially proposes as a seduction strategy — is an efficient character joke. The logic is absurdist but internally consistent for him.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm the king of the world!

jokes.text: Ben: 'I can't believe I'm about to be the mayor.' Garry: 'I can't believe I'm about to notarize it.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Garry share a parallel moment of awe before the mayoral signing
jokes.punchline: Ben's historic personal moment is matched in scale by Garry's notarizing excitement — both are equally awed by very different things
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure of 'I can't believe I'm about to be the mayor' / 'I can't believe I'm about to notarize it' is a clean bit. Garry's sincere excitement about notarizing has the same emotional weight as Ben becoming mayor. The equality of their enthusiasm is the joke.

jokes.text: Ben and Garry's excitement about notarizing the new mayor: 'I can't believe I'm about to be the mayor.' / 'I can't believe I'm about to notarize it.'
jokes.setup: Ben is preparing to sign as interim mayor
jokes.punchline: Garry's parallel excitement about notarizing matches Ben's excitement about becoming mayor — to Garry, these are equal thrills
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure of 'I can't believe I'm about to X' with mayor/notarize as the two equal thrills is perfect. Garry's sincere passion for notarizing elevated to the same plane as holding public office is deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Ben decides not to be mayor and reflects: 'I like that Ice Town happened, and I don't want to erase it.' / Garry: 'Okay, I wasn't listening to anything you just said. But who is gonna be the mayor for the next two months, then?'
jokes.setup: Ben has a meaningful personal moment about accepting his past
jokes.punchline: Garry immediately admits he wasn't listening — deflating the emotional moment with complete guilelessness
jokes.explanation: Garry's admission is disarmingly honest rather than cruel. He's not dismissing Ben; he just genuinely wasn't listening and needs the practical information. The contrast between Ben's growth moment and Garry's practical indifference is the joke.

jokes.text: Leslie offers the mayorship to Garry Gergich — who screams 'NO!' in abject terror before presumably accepting
jokes.setup: After everyone else has declined, Leslie turns to Garry as the choice for interim mayor
jokes.punchline: Garry's immediate 'No!' — a man who has spent his career being minimized, now terrified by the honor he should want
jokes.explanation: The 'No!' gets its own timestamp, suggesting a deliberate comedy pause. Garry's instinctive rejection of the honor he's spent his career being denied is perfectly absurd. The brevity — one word, beat, cut — is structurally perfect. And context tells us he'll accept, making the 'No!' even funnier.

jokes.text: Tom's simple proposal at The Snakehole Lounge: recreating their first date with a daisy, a failed magic trick, and a card pick — Lucy says yes.
jokes.setup: Tom's elaborate action-movie proposal was abandoned; now he's at the bar where they met with minimal props
jokes.punchline: The magic trick still fails — 'I haven't done this trick in a while' — but Lucy says yes anyway. The comedy is in the earnest failure being more romantic than the spectacle.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is gentle — the failed magic trick as the authentic proposal is sweet and quietly funny. The contrast with the elaborate failed proposal earlier is the true punchline. Works as character payoff even if not a hard laugh.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio responds to Tom's engagement by immediately hitting on Lucy: 'So what's your story again? I mean, like, how married are you? You down to clown? You in that rude mood?' / 'Why are you like this?' / 'Pills, baby!'
jokes.setup: Tom just got engaged. Jean-Ralphio congratulates them.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio immediately tries to pick up the newly-engaged woman with increasingly deranged questions — 'You in that rude mood?' — then explains himself with 'Pills, baby!'
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio at his absolute best. 'How married are you?' and 'You in that rude mood?' are perfectly calibrated terrible pickup lines. 'Pills, baby!' as his entire self-explanation is iconic — it's simultaneously a joke, a character description, and an excuse all in two words. Highly quotable, fully character-specific, and lands with impact. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Donna convinces Typhoon (a new barber) to cut Ron's hair by promising it'll take four minutes and cost $8. Ron's only input: she shows him a photo of what he wants to look like.
jokes.setup: Ron needs a new barber. Donna has found Typhoon, an avant-garde artist barber.
jokes.punchline: Ron's desired look is a photo of himself — he wants to look exactly as he already does, no change whatsoever
jokes.explanation: The visual punchline — Ron showing a photo of himself as the desired result — is the logical endpoint of his entire character philosophy about consistency and avoiding change. It's a visual joke that only works because of years of character building. High character integration score is fully justified.

jokes.text: Typhoon: 'I'm writing an electronic opera about Brittany Murphy, and I do the chandelier design for my friend's drag puppet show.' / 'No further questions.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks Typhoon what he does for fun, as a small-talk attempt from Ron (already unusual)
jokes.punchline: Typhoon's answer is so specific and alien to Ron that he immediately terminates the conversation — 'No further questions' as a formal closing
jokes.explanation: Typhoon's answer is perfectly calibrated weirdness — both specific items (electronic opera about Brittany Murphy, chandelier design for drag puppet shows) are genuinely funny in their specificity. Ron's 'No further questions' as a formal termination of curiosity is the ideal Ron response.

jokes.text: Typhoon: 'Except lately all the good warehouse raves are filled with Eurotrash.' / Ron: '"Eurotrash," I like that. It is, indeed, a garbage continent.'
jokes.setup: Typhoon laments his social scene; Ron has just said 'No further questions'
jokes.punchline: Ron re-engages only because Typhoon said something Ron can agree with — his anti-European sentiment creating an unlikely bond
jokes.explanation: 'It is, indeed, a garbage continent' is a beautifully absurd piece of Ron Swanson logic — his European skepticism extended to continental dismissal. The pivot from 'No further questions' to immediate engagement over this is perfect character comedy. The phrase is highly quotable.

jokes.text: Typhoon complains about Berlin: 'Everyone was on their stupid bikes. I was like, "Ew."' / Ron: 'Please, talk more about how you hate Europe and bicycles.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Typhoon are bonding over disliking Europe
jokes.punchline: Ron explicitly requests more of this — 'Please, talk more about how you hate Europe and bicycles' — his anti-Europe and anti-bicycle sentiments perfectly aligned with a drag-puppet-show barber
jokes.explanation: 'Please, talk more about how you hate Europe and bicycles' is a precise summary of Ron's established character preferences. The joy of this scene is that Ron's most antisocial qualities create an unlikely connection with the most avant-garde character imaginable. Character integration is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'll see you later, Jennifer Knopez.' / Leslie: 'Catch you on the flip side, Tom-egranate Juice.' / Tom: 'Hey, not bad.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie say goodbye after the engagement
jokes.punchline: They exchange nickname portmanteaus — Tom's is professional, Leslie's ('Tom-egranate Juice') earns genuine approval from Tom
jokes.explanation: 'Tom-egranate Juice' is a genuinely creative portmanteau — pomegranate juice as a Tom pun earns its keep. Tom's approving 'Hey, not bad' is a nice character beat — Tom's branding expertise applied to Leslie's name. Warm and functional.

jokes.text: Tom and Leslie say goodbye with food-pun nicknames: 'Jennifer Knopez' / 'Tom-egranate Juice' — 'Hey, not bad.'
jokes.setup: Tom tells Leslie he'll see her later as he leaves with Lucy
jokes.punchline: They exchange food-themed nickname portmanteaus — 'Jennifer Knopez' (J-Lo / Knope) and 'Tom-egranate Juice' — Tom grades Leslie's effort: 'Hey, not bad.'
jokes.explanation: Tom's nickname habit is a long-running character trait. 'Tom-egranate Juice' is a good portmanteau, and Leslie getting a 'not bad' from Tom — who invented this art form — is a sweet, funny beat. Character-specific and warm.

jokes.text: April: 'Oh, so glad we're leaving.' (after hearing Garry is mayor)
jokes.setup: Leslie announces Garry will be the mayor
jokes.punchline: April's immediate, unguarded relief at leaving before Garry's mayorship is a perfect character reaction
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional April reaction beat. The brevity and sincerity make it land. Not a crafted joke so much as a character-true response.

jokes.text: Leslie calls the banner store owner, says 'Ian, thank you so much. It's great. Now throw it out. I need a new one, and I need it in 20 minutes.'
jokes.setup: Ian made the Congratulations Tom and Lucy banner Leslie ordered
jokes.punchline: She immediately discards it the moment it's done and orders a new one — casual waste of his emergency labor
jokes.explanation: Pays off the earlier banner store scenes. Leslie's relationship with Ian as a source of emergency banner labor — discarded the moment circumstances change — is good character comedy. The 'throw it out' after the effort is the comedic gut punch.

jokes.text: 'Look, if you didn't want to be on call 24-7 for emergencies, then you should not have gone into the high-stakes world of banner making!'
jokes.setup: Ian protests the impossible last-minute request to replace the banner
jokes.punchline: Leslie frames banner making as a high-stakes emergency profession where 24/7 availability is an occupational expectation
jokes.explanation: 'The high-stakes world of banner making' is one of the episode's best lines. The absurdity of treating sign-printing as emergency medicine is perfectly Leslie — her needs are always life-or-death, and she's extended that worldview to her vendors. Highly quotable, character-perfect, and the phrase construction is excellent.

jokes.text: Garry walks into his office to find a full inauguration party — 'Happy Inauguration Day, buddy.' Garry: 'Oh, jeez, Leslie.'
jokes.setup: Garry has reluctantly accepted the interim mayorship
jokes.punchline: Leslie has thrown a full inauguration party. Garry's 'Oh, jeez, Leslie' — part overwhelmed, part embarrassed, all Garry — is the emotional-comedy button
jokes.explanation: More of an emotional payoff than a hard joke, but it functions comedically through Garry's helpless response to Leslie's overwhelming thoughtfulness. Works as comedy because we understand both characters.

jokes.text: Garry's first act as mayor: he starts crying at the podium, finally says 'I'm flying!' while overcome with emotion
jokes.setup: Garry is introduced as the new mayor of Pawnee; he starts to speak
jokes.punchline: After a long emotional pause, his only words are 'I'm flying!' — absurd, joyful, and perfectly Garry
jokes.explanation: The episode's emotional and comedic climax. The long pause (implied by the timestamp gap from 21:00 to 21:13) builds tension; 'I'm flying!' is the perfect release — absurd, joyful, childlike. It captures everything about Garry: earnest, overwhelmed, not eloquent but genuine. The episode's most earned laugh because it's also touching. Economy is exceptional — two words deliver the scene's entire payload. Among the episode's very best moments.
